Empirical Research Plan  
“Financial Development, Financial Dependence, and Industry Growth, 1980-1990”  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design: Difference-in-Differences in triple-interaction (sometimes called a “generalized DID” or “difference-in-difference-in-differences”).

Rationale:  
• We observe annual panels for industry i in country c over time t.  
• Financial development (FD_ct) varies across countries and years; financial dependence (FDep_i) is time-invariant and measured once (e.g., in U.S. data).  
• The interaction FD_ct × FDep_i captures whether industries that *need* outside finance grow faster when, in a given year, their country’s financial system is deeper.  
• With a rich set of fixed effects (country-year, industry-year, and country-industry) the identifying variation is *within* a country-year, comparing high- vs. low-dependence industries, and *within* an industry-year, comparing more vs. less financially developed countries.  
• Parallel-trends style assumptions are testable in pre-periods, and we can augment with an IV for FD_ct if desired.

Mathematically:

Growth_ict = β (FDep_i × FD_ct) + α_ci + γ_it + λ_ct + ε_ict

β is the causal effect of financial development on the growth of an industry whose external financial dependence equals one unit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable:  
T_ict = FDep_i × FD_ct

• FDep_i: industry’s external‐finance dependence; standardized (0–1).  
• FD_ct: country-year financial development; e.g., private-credit-to-GDP, stock-market capitalization/GDP, or first PC of several measures.

Who is “treated”? In a given country-year, industries with higher FDep_i receive a higher “dose” of treatment when FD_ct is high.

Control group (counterfactual):  
• Low-dependence industries in the same country-year.  
• High-dependence industries in a country-year with low financial development.

Treatment timing: continuous; we exploit the annual evolution 1980-1990.

No single cutoff → no RDD.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends (conditional): In the absence of changes in FD_ct, growth differences between high- and low-dependence industries within a country would have evolved in parallel.

Plausibility: We include country-industry and industry-year fixed effects to soak up time-invariant technology shocks and global industry shocks. Short ten-year window further helps.

A2. Exogeneity of Financial Dependence: FDep_i is pre-determined and not influenced by country-specific shocks during 1980-1990.

Plausibility: We measure FDep_i using data from a large external market (e.g., U.S. 1970s) and treat it as technological.

A3. No Simultaneous Policies Correlated with FD_ct that Differentially Favor High-dependence Industries.

Plausibility: Could be violated if, for instance, trade liberalization and financial reform occur together. We will control for plausible concurrent reforms (trade openness, exchange-rate regime).

A4. No General-Equilibrium Spillovers: Growth of one industry does not crowd out others within the same country in a way that biases relative comparisons.

Plausibility: Less likely at ten-year horizon but cannot be ruled out. We test robustness using value-added shares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Reverse Causality: Booming high-dependence industries might induce policies that deepen finance, biasing β upward.

Fix: Instrument FD_ct with plausibly exogenous drivers: (i) legal origin dummies × time trends, (ii) lagged global interest-rate shocks interacted with dollarization, (iii) occurrence of banking-sector deregulation dated by external sources. Implement 2SLS.

T2. Omitted Simultaneous Reforms: Trade, privatization, or macro stabilization could co-move with FD_ct and matter more for high-dependence industries.

Fix: Add controls Trade_ct × FDep_i, Privatization_ct × FDep_i, etc. Drop years around big macro events as sensitivity.

T3. Measurement Error in FD_ct or growth rates, especially in developing countries.

Fix: Use multiple FD measures, construct an index by PCA, winsorize outliers, do errors-in-variables correction via IV.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional FE
library(multiwayvcov) # for two-way clustering
library(readr)

# ---- 1. Load Data ----
# Assume three csv files: industry_growth.csv, financial_dev.csv, fin_depend.csv
grow  <- fread("industry_growth.csv")   # columns: country, year, industry, growth
fdev  <- fread("financial_dev.csv")     # columns: country, year, fd
fdep  <- fread("fin_depend.csv")        # columns: industry, fdep

# ---- 2. Merge & Construct Variables ----
DT <- merge(grow, fdev,  by = c("country","year"))
DT <- merge(DT, fdep,    by = "industry")
DT[, treat := fd * fdep]               # interaction
# Standardize
DT[, fdep_z := scale(fdep)]
DT[, fd_z   := scale(fd)]
DT[, treat_z:= fd_z * fdep_z]

# ---- 3. Baseline Triple-Diff Regression ----
est1 <- feols(growth ~ treat_z | country^industry + industry^year + country^year,
              data = DT, cluster = ~country + industry)  # two-way clustering
summary(est1)

# ---- 4. Instrumental Variable Version ----
# Example instrument: legal_origin (time-invariant) × global_time_trend
# Assume pre-loaded variable legal_origin_common
DT[, z_fd := legal_origin_common * year]  # simplified illustration
est2 <- feols(growth ~ 1 | country^industry + industry^year + country^year 
               | treat_z ~ z_fd*fdep_z,      # first-stage: fd_z instrumented
               data = DT, cluster = ~country + industry)
summary(est2)

# ---- 5. Robustness: Alt. FD measure & Placebo ----
# (a) Use stock-market cap/GDP
DT[, treat_alt := stock_mkt_cap * fdep_z]
rob1 <- feols(growth ~ treat_alt | country^industry + industry^year + country^year,
              data = DT, cluster = ~country + industry)
summary(rob1)

# (b) Placebo: interact 5-year *pre* period trend with fdep
DT[, pre_period := (year <= 1980)]
DT[, placebo := pre_period * fdep_z]
placebo_est <- feols(growth ~ placebo | country^industry + industry^year + country^year,
                     data = DT, cluster = ~country + industry)
summary(placebo_est)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (credit constraints) predicts β > 0: industries that rely heavily on external funds benefit more when local financial markets are deeper. A one-SD increase in FD_ct is expected to raise the annual growth rate of a one-SD higher-dependence industry by roughly 0.3-0.6 pp. Magnitude benchmark: Rajan & Zingales (1998) find ~0.7 pp for 1980-1990.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Difference-in-Differences)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)

C1: Pre-treatment Parallel Trends demonstrably hold within country-industry pairs … 0.8  
C2: No simultaneous shocks violating exclusion … 0.6  
C3: Stable composition of industries (entry/exit not biasing) … 0.9  
C4: Correct standard-error clustering & inference … 1  
C5: No interference/spillovers across units … 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.8 → design reasonably credible but not bullet-proof; IV robustness is essential.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of proposed empirical plan
